items.summary:
### Summary

This is a residual of GHSA-g5vv-9gxw-82hx / CVE-2026-87819. The 3.1.60 fix made `Actor._from_string` regex-free, but `parse_actor_and_date` still runs `_re_actor_epoch` on the same author/committer/tagger line one step earlier. That pattern backtracks quadratically when the trailing epoch or timezone is missing or malformed, so the same class of slow parse is still reachable in 3.1.62.

### Details

`git/objects/util.py:322`:

```python
_re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.+? (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$")
```

`.+?` and `(.*)` can both absorb the same run of spaces, and the required ` (\d+) ([+-]\d+)` tail is only checked after them. On a long line with no valid tail, the search retries every split point.

It is called from `parse_actor_and_date` (`git/objects/util.py:335`), which runs on the author and committer lines in `Commit._deserialize` (`git/objects/commit.py:917`, `:931`) and on the tagger line in `git/objects/tag.py:129`.

The published payload (letters plus an unterminated `<`) is fast on 3.1.62. Replacing the letters with spaces is not:

| author line (after `author `) | 2 KB | 8 KB | 32 KB |
|---|---|---|---|
| `'a'*n + ' <'` (advisory payload) | 0.0 ms | 0.1 ms | 0.4 ms |
| `' '*n` | 28 ms | 453 ms | 7,700 ms |
| valid line, long name (control) | 0.0 ms | 0.0 ms | 0.0 ms |

Cost grows about 16x for each 4x increase in length.

### PoC

```python
import time
from git.objects.util import parse_actor_and_date

line = "author " + " " * 32000
t = time.perf_counter()
parse_actor_and_date(line)
print(f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.1f} s")   # ~7 s on 3.1.62
```

End to end, reading `Commit.author` on a commit object whose author line is 32 KB of spaces followed by any malformed tail (no epoch, no timezone, non-numeric epoch, or bad timezone) takes about 7.2 s per access. The same line with a valid `1191999972 -0700` tail takes 1.3 ms.

Note for reproducing: `git hash-object -t commit -w` refuses such an object (`missingEmail`), so the test object was written with `--literally`. A remote can still serve one, because `fetch.fsckObjects` and `transfer.fsckObjects` default to false. This is the same delivery model as CVE-2026-87819 ("craft a commit object with a malformed author field").

### Impact

CPU exhaustion (CWE-1333) in any application that uses GitPython to read commits or tags from an untrusted repository: CI tooling, repository scanners, code-hosting integrations. Each access to `Commit.author`, `Commit.committer` or `TagObject.tagger` on a crafted object costs seconds, and a repository can contain many such objects.

### Suggested fix

Match the leading field name with `.[^ ]*` instead of `.+?`. Both stop at the first space after the first character, but `.[^ ]*` cannot overlap the following `(.*)`, so the backtracking disappears:

```python
_re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$")
_re_only_actor = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*)$")
```

Verification on current main (73a72c9):

- Differential over 368 actor lines (real-world shapes plus edge cases): 0 differences in match groups for either regex.
- `' '*n` at 64 KB: 32,170 ms before, 0.98 ms after. Valid lines are unchanged (0.01 ms).
- The existing test suite gives the same pass/fail set with and without the change
- The new regression test, `test_parse_actor_and_date_malformed_line_is_linear`, fails on the old pattern (8.4 s) and passes with the fix (0.5 s).

The full patch (fix plus regression test) is attached below.

```diff
diff --git a/git/objects/util.py b/git/objects/util.py
index a68d701f..d8c0594d 100644
--- a/git/objects/util.py
+++ b/git/objects/util.py
@@ -319,8 +319,11 @@ def parse_date(string_date: Union[str, datetime]) -> Tuple[int, int]:
 
 
 # Precompiled regexes
-_re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.+? (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$")
-_re_only_actor = re.compile(r"^.+? (.*)$")
+# The leading field name ("author", "committer", "tagger") is matched with ``.[^ ]*`` rather than
+# ``.+?``: both stop at the first space after the first character, but ``.[^ ]*`` cannot overlap the
+# following ``(.*)``, so a line with no valid trailing epoch/offset no longer backtracks quadratically.
+_re_actor_epoch = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*) (\d+) ([+-]\d+).*$")
+_re_only_actor = re.compile(r"^.[^ ]* (.*)$")
 
 
 def parse_actor_and_date(line: str) -> Tuple[Actor, int, int]:
diff --git a/test/test_util.py b/test/test_util.py
index cf4299d5..e1631420 100644
--- a/test/test_util.py
+++ b/test/test_util.py
@@ -22,6 +22,7 @@ from git.cmd import dashify
 from git.objects.util import (
     altz_to_utctz_str,
     from_timestamp,
+    parse_actor_and_date,
     parse_date,
     tzoffset,
     utctz_to_altz,
@@ -571,6 +572,30 @@ class TestUtils(TestBase):
             Actor("name last another", "some-very-long-email@example.com"),
         )
 
+    def test_parse_actor_and_date_malformed_line_is_linear(self):
+        # A long author line whose trailing epoch/offset is missing or malformed used to make
+        # _re_actor_epoch backtrack quadratically: ~7 s per Commit.author access for a 32 KB line.
+        # The parse result must be unchanged; only the time spent reaching it should move.
+        for tail in ("", " notanumber -0700", " 1191999972", " -0700", " 1191999972 xx"):
+            line = "author " + " " * 32000 + tail
+            start = time.perf_counter()
+            actor, epoch, offset = parse_actor_and_date(line)
+            self.assertLess(time.perf_counter() - start, 1.0)
+            self.assertEqual(epoch, 0)
+            self.assertEqual(offset, 0)
+
+        # Well-formed lines, including one with a long name, still parse exactly as before.
+        actor, epoch, offset = parse_actor_and_date(
+            "author Tom Preston-Werner <tom@mojombo.com> 1191999972 -0700"
+        )
+        self.assertEqual(actor, Actor("Tom Preston-Werner", "tom@mojombo.com"))
+        self.assertEqual(epoch, 1191999972)
+        self.assertEqual(offset, 25200)
+
+        actor, epoch, offset = parse_actor_and_date("author " + "a " * 16000 + "<a@b> 1 -0700")
+        self.assertEqual(actor.email, "a@b")
+        self.assertEqual(epoch, 1)
+
     @ddt.data(
         ("name", ""),
         ("name", "prefix_"),
```

Found with AI assistance (Claude) and verified by hand.

Brian Willows

items.summary: When pretix is used as the identity provider in a Single-Sign-On (SSO) setup for customer accounts, the system did not properly validate the `response_type` requested in an authorization request against the configured grant type of the SSO client. This means that if an SSO client was configured to only allow the `code` response type, which requires knowledge of the client secret to use and would wrongfully send a response type like `id_token`, it would receive back a valid token. Exploiting this requires the attacker to run JavaScript on the page specified by `redirect_uri`, which must be from a list specified in the client configuration.

items.summary: Axel Download Accelerator 2.17.14 and earlier performs URL percent-decoding (http_decode()) on the output filename after the URL has been parsed and the filename component extracted. This allows an attacker to embed %2e%2e%2f (URL-encoded ../) sequences in the URL path. These sequences survive the URL parser intact (they contain no literal / characters) but are decoded into directory traversal sequences before the output file is opened for writing. As a result, a crafted URL can cause axel to write downloaded content to arbitrary filesystem paths relative to the current working directory.

items.summary:
> **A note on the referenced files.** This report was submitted through GitHub's private
> vulnerability reporting API, which carries no attachments. Every transcript this report leans
> on is reproduced **inline above**, verbatim. The file names it mentions (`poc.sh`, `poc.log`,
> per-case transcripts, `evidence.md`, `negative-controls.md`, blob-sweep tables) are the local
> evidence bundle those inline excerpts were extracted from, with a checksum manifest. I am happy
> to send the bundle by any channel you prefer, or to open a private fork — just say which. The
> PoC scripts are self-contained and reproduce the result from a clean environment.

---

**Affected:** `<= 3.1.62` — all published releases; also `main` @ `4905b4af`
**Verified at runtime:** GitPython `3.1.62` with git `2.55.0`
**Date:** 2026-09-10
**Reporter:** MAXI8594

---

## Threat model

| | |
|---|---|
| **Attacker** | anyone who can get the application to clone a URL they control. No account, no credential, no privilege in the consuming application. |
| **Pre-need** | a repository they host, with `HEAD` pointing at a branch whose name is the payload. A `git push` to a plain git server is enough — no filesystem access to a server is required (`raw/06`). |
| **Gets** | the contents of any file the application's process can read, returned in band through the exception. `/etc/passwd` recovered 34 of 34 lines. |
| **Real-world likelihood** | **High.** The vulnerable consumer is six lines of ordinary code with no unusual configuration: `Repo.clone_from(user_url)` then `repo.active_branch.checkout()`. `allow_unsafe_options=False` is the default. Cloning user-supplied URLs is the library's central use case — CI systems, repository importers, scanners and bots. |

**On severity relative to the sibling advisories.** GitHub, as CNA, scored the three prior
advisories in this class at 6.5 / `PR:L` (CVE-2026-76217, CVE-2026-78678, CVE-2026-78679). This
report asks for 7.5 / `PR:N`, and the difference is one measured fact: in those three, the
application had to pass an attacker-influenced value into the API. Here it passes nothing — the
clone materialises the hostile branch on its own and `repo.active_branch` returns it
(`raw/02`). If that reading is not accepted, the `PR:L` path via `Repo.create_head()` is also real
and lands at 6.5, matching the siblings.

## Summary

`Head.checkout()` guards its `**kwargs` against unsafe Git options but never inspects its own
positional argument — the branch name — which reaches the `git checkout` argv with no `--`
separator. A repository whose default branch is named `--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd` makes a
consumer that merely clones it and checks out the default branch return the entire contents of that
file to the caller.

This is the exact combination of two advisories the project already fixed:

- **CVE-2026-76217** (`GHSA-hh9p-6wh2-4mfc`) — *"Arbitrary file read via `--pathspec-from-file` in
  `IndexFile.remove()` **and `Head.checkout()`**"*. Fixed in 3.1.58 by commit `f2550b65`, which added
  the guard to this exact method — but only for `**kwargs`.
- **CVE-2026-78679** (`GHSA-3wxw-xv34-2frg`) — *"`TagReference.create` positional reference
  bypasses kwargs-only `--file` guard, enabling arbitrary file read (incomplete fix of 3af0c251)"*. Fixed in 3.1.59 by commit `1b0d2d9b`, which applied the
  positional check to `git/refs/tag.py`, `git/diff.py`, `git/index/base.py` and `git/repo/base.py` —
  but not to `git/refs/head.py:286`.

`f2550b65` states in its own commit message that the audit found the positional variant and applied
it to `HEAD.reset` — 185 lines above `Head.checkout`, in the same file, in the same commit:

> "The audit also found that **reset's positional commit could carry the option before its argument
> separator**. […] **Check reset's positional commit as well as keyword options**"

`HEAD.reset` got the fix. `Head.checkout` did not, and `1b0d2d9b` did not come back for it.

## Affected Asset

| | |
|---|---|
| Package | `GitPython` (PyPI) |
| Affected versions | **`<= 3.1.62`** — all published releases |
| Latest release tested | `3.1.62` |
| Also present on | `main` @ `4905b4af` |
| Vulnerable file | `git/refs/head.py` |
| Guard | line 286 — `Git._option_candidates([], kwargs)` |
| Sink | line 293 — `self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs)` |
| CWE | CWE-88 (Argument Injection), CWE-73 (External Control of File Name or Path), CWE-200 (Exposure of Sensitive Information) |
| CVSS 3.1 | `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N` → **7.5 High** |

The version range was established by **blob hash against every tag**, not by dates: the sink line
`self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs)` — with no `--` separator — is present in `git/refs/head.py`
in every tag from `0.3.1-beta2` through `3.1.62`. The `3.1.62` blob is byte-identical to `main`:
`7f563374ef9e018b3d5f95054498e8591e112ce2`. Full sweep in `raw/07-blob-version-sweep.txt`.

The kwargs-only guard first appears in **3.1.58**, so `3.1.58`–`3.1.62` is where "incomplete fix"
applies; earlier releases have the same sink with no guard at all.

## Vulnerability Details

### Root cause

`git/cmd.py:1045` — `_option_candidates()` only inspects the positionals it is handed:

```python
@classmethod
def _option_candidates(cls, args: Sequence[Any] = (), kwargs: Optional[Mapping[str, Any]] = None) -> List[str]:
    """Collect possible option spellings before command-line transformation."""
    options = [
        option for option in cls._unpack_args([arg for arg in args if arg is not None]) if option.startswith("-")
    ]
```

So `_option_candidates([], kwargs)` means: *check the keyword arguments, never check the positional
arguments this method puts on the command line.* That is fine when the method has no
attacker-influenced positional, or when it separates them with `--`.

`git/refs/head.py:283-293` — `Head.checkout()` has neither:

```python
        if not allow_unsafe_options:
            Git.check_unsafe_options(
                options=Git._option_candidates([], kwargs),
                unsafe_options=Git.unsafe_git_pathspec_from_file_options,
            )
        kwargs["f"] = force
        if kwargs["f"] is False:
            kwargs.pop("f")

        self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs)
```

`self` is the only positional. It serialises to the branch name, lands in the `git checkout` argv,
and is not in the list the guard inspects. `_call_process` builds `args_list = opt_args + ext_args`,
so keyword-derived options precede positionals — which is why the rest of the library puts `"--"`
first (`Remote.fetch/pull/push`, `Repo._clone`, `Repo.archive`, `IndexFile.remove`, `Commit.count`
all do). `Head.checkout` does not.

### Why the branch name is attacker-controlled

Git accepts a refname whose branch component begins with `-` and contains `/`
(`raw/02-refname-accepted-and-cloned.txt`):

```
>>> git check-ref-format 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'
    exit=0  stderr=''
    => un refname que empieza con '-' y lleva '/' es VALIDO para git

>>> git -C <bare> update-ref 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd' beea87239099
    exit=0  stderr=''
>>> git -C <bare> symbolic-ref HEAD 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'
    exit=0
    HEAD del bare = refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd
    ref en disco como arbol jerarquico: True

>>> Repo.clone_from('file://<bare>', <victim>)   # la app solo clona
    ramas LOCALES creadas por el clone, sin que nadie las pida:
      refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd
    repo.active_branch.name = '--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'
    coincide con el nombre hostil: True
```

The transcript above also shows the second half: `git clone` **materialises that branch locally on
its own** when the remote `HEAD` points at it — the consuming application never asks for it.

A plain git server accepts the refname over `receive-pack`, with no `--force` and no special config
(`raw/06-push-accepts-refname.txt`), so the attacker does not need filesystem access to a server —
a `git push` is enough. That measurement, and the clone in `raw/02`, both use the `file://`
transport, which exercises the same git wire protocol as `https://`; I did not test against a
hosted forge, since that would mean writing to a third party.

### Why the leak reaches the caller

The file contents are in `CommandError.__str__`, not only in the `.stderr` attribute
(`git/exc.py`):

```python
        self.stderr = stderr_decode and "\n  stderr: '%s'" % stderr_decode or ""

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return (self._msg + "\n  cmdline: %s%s%s") % (
            self._cmd, self._cause, self._cmdline, self.stdout, self.stderr,
        )
```

So `logging.exception(...)`, `print(e)`, or simply **not catching** the exception all disclose the
file. The developer does not have to know `.stderr` exists.

### Full chain

```
Repo.clone_from(<attacker URL>)
  ↓  remote HEAD points at refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd
  ↓  git clone creates that LOCAL branch unasked
repo.active_branch                → Head with name = "--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd"
  ↓
Head.checkout()                   git/refs/head.py:286 — guard inspects kwargs only
  ↓  self.repo.git.checkout(self, **kwargs)   git/refs/head.py:293 — no "--"
git checkout --pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd
  ↓  git emits one `error:` per unmatched pathspec — one per line of the file
GitCommandError → CommandError.__str__ → the consumer
```

## Steps to Reproduce

Environment: GitPython 3.1.62, git 2.55.0, Linux x86_64, disposable venv. Everything local —
temporary repositories and the `file://` transport. No remote hosts, no third-party repositories.

The bundled `poc.sh` runs all seven scenarios as a single unit and writes `poc.log` plus one file per
scenario under `raw/`. Minimal manual reproduction:

```bash
python3 -m venv /tmp/gp && /tmp/gp/bin/python -m pip install gitpython==3.1.62

W=$(mktemp -d)
git init -q -b main "$W/a"; echo x > "$W/a/f.txt"
git -C "$W/a" add f.txt
git -C "$W/a" -c user.email=a@b -c user.name=a commit -qm c
git clone -q --bare "$W/a" "$W/a.git"
SHA=$(git -C "$W/a.git" rev-parse HEAD)

# the attacker names their default branch after the file they want
git -C "$W/a.git" update-ref   'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd' "$SHA"
git -C "$W/a.git" symbolic-ref HEAD 'refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'

cat > "$W/consumer.py" <<'PYEOF'
import logging, sys, git
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(message)s")
try:
    repo = git.Repo.clone_from(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])   # user-supplied URL
    repo.active_branch.checkout()                          # ensure a clean working tree
except git.exc.GitCommandError:
    logging.exception("clone failed")
PYEOF

/tmp/gp/bin/python "$W/consumer.py" "file://$W/a.git" "$W/victim"
```

### Raw Request

The real `git checkout` argv, captured by instrumenting `Git.execute` (`raw/01-real-argv.txt`).
This is the command GitPython actually built — the branch name became an option:

```
  argv real : ['git', 'checkout', '--pathspec-from-file=/tmp/gpargv-9im8ao2d/SECRET.txt']
```

### Raw Response

Observed output (`raw/05-six-line-consumer.txt`, tail) — git emits one `error:` line per unmatched
pathspec, which is one per line of the target file:

```
error: pathspec 'mysql:x:958:958:MariaDB:/var/lib/mysql:/usr/bin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git
error: pathspec 'flatpak:x:957:957:Flatpak system helper:/:/usr/bin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git
error: pathspec 'wazuh:x:956:955:Wazuh Agent:/var/ossec:/usr/sbin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git
error: pathspec 'jdownloader:x:955:954:jdownloader:/opt/JDownloader/:/bin/false' did not match any file(s) known to git
error: pathspec 'cups-browsed:x:953:953:CUPS printer discovery:/:/usr/bin/nologin' did not match any file(s) known to git'
```

`raw/03-full-file-disclosure.txt` counts the recovery against the real file:

```
Archivo objetivo: /etc/passwd  (34 lineas no vacias)
[CASO] repo.active_branch.checkout()  — nadie paso un nombre de rama
  repo.active_branch.name = '--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd'
  -> GitCommandError. Lineas de /etc/passwd recuperadas: 34 de 34
```

## Impact

An attacker who can get an application to clone a repository they control reads any file the
application's process can read, with the contents returned in band. `/etc/passwd` was recovered in
full (34 of 34 lines) in the run recorded in `poc.log`.

The attacker needs **no account and no privilege in the consuming application**, and no
configuration change anywhere: `allow_unsafe_options=False` is the default, and the vulnerable
consumer is six lines of ordinary code. This is the central use case of the library — CI systems,
repository importers, scanners and bots that clone user-supplied URLs.

### Impact precondition

**Holds if:** the consuming application clones a repository whose default branch name the attacker
chose, and then calls `Head.checkout()` on it — most commonly as `repo.active_branch.checkout()`,
which needs no branch-name input from the application at all.

**Source writer:** the attacker, via the remote repository's `HEAD` and refs. Verified two ways —
`git update-ref` + `symbolic-ref` on a bare repository, and `git push` to a plain git server, which
`receive-pack` accepts without `--force` or special configuration
(`raw/02-refname-accepted-and-cloned.txt`, `raw/06-push-accepts-refname.txt`). The application never
writes the branch name; `git clone` materialises it.

**Observed in:** `validation/gitpython/head-checkout-positional-pathspec/` — GitPython 3.1.62
(latest release) with git 2.55.0, in the single run recorded in `poc.log`
(2026-09-10T02:10:23-03:00). File read: `/etc/passwd`, 34 of 34 lines recovered by the caller.


### Limits, stated plainly

- Only the full long spelling works, because a refname cannot contain a space and is therefore a
  single argv token; `git` rejects the abbreviated forms. This was established while developing the
  payload and is **not** part of the attached run — the run exercises the working spelling only.
- The attacker must know an absolute path to the target file.
- Lines are disclosed only when they do not match a path in the repository. With a one-file hostile
  repository none of them do, so the attacker controls this condition too.
- The full-file result was measured on **git 2.55.0**, where `git checkout` emits one `error:` per
  unmatched pathspec. `GHSA-hh9p-6wh2-4mfc` notes that `--pathspec-from-file` alone quotes only the
  first line — that holds for `git rm`, which aborts with `fatal:` on the first. It does not hold for
  `git checkout` on 2.55.0.

## Negative control

Full statement of what each control isolates and what would invalidate it: `negative-controls.md`.
Every batch opens **and closes** with a positive control; if the closing one does not fire, the batch
is discarded.

**Positive control (opening and closing, 4 batches).** `Head.checkout(pathspec_from_file="/etc/passwd")`
— the same payload via kwargs. Fires in every batch:
`UnsafeOptionError: --pathspec-from-file is not allowed, use allow_unsafe_options=True to allow it`.
This proves the guard exists, is active under the default, and recognises the option — so a null
result elsewhere cannot be the instrument failing to reach the code.

**Negative control.** The identical call on a branch named `benigna`. One variable changes: the
leading `-`. Result: `['git', 'checkout', 'benigna']`, no exception, 0 lines disclosed.

**Precision control — the asymmetry inside one file** (`raw/04-precision-control-reset-vs-checkout.txt`).
The same payload against the two methods in `git/refs/head.py` that received the guard in the same
commit, 185 lines apart:

```
[CONTROL DE PRECISION] mismo archivo, mismo commit de fix, dos metodos
  HEAD.reset(commit=PAYLOAD)  guard SI mira el posicional BLOQUEADO por el guard (--pathspec-from-file i fuga= 0 lineas  [OK]
  Head.checkout()      guard NO mira el posicional     GitCommandError                                fuga=34 lineas  [OK]
```

`HEAD.reset` (`head.py:101`, `_option_candidates([commit], kwargs)`) blocks what `Head.checkout`
(`head.py:286`, `_option_candidates([], kwargs)`) lets through. This rules out the alternative
explanation that any string containing `--pathspec-from-file` reaching git would disclose the file.

## Remediation

One line, consistent with what `f2550b65` already did for `HEAD.reset` in this same file:

```python
                options=Git._option_candidates([self], kwargs),
```

**The other candidate was evaluated and rejected.** Writing
`self.repo.git.checkout("--", self, **kwargs)` would match the `--` pattern used elsewhere in the
library and would also cover future `git checkout` options — but it **changes the semantics and
breaks the method**: in `git checkout -- <arg>`, everything after `--` is a *pathspec*, not a branch.
The command would stop switching branches and start restoring files. The `--` pattern works for
`fetch`/`pull`/`push`/`clone`/`archive`/`rm` because their positionals genuinely are non-branch
operands; it does not transfer here.

For defence in depth, `Repo.create_head()` could reject branch names beginning with `-`, which would
also close the weaker `PR:L` path. That is a separate, optional change.

## Prior art and de-duplication

All GitPython advisories in the GitHub database were reviewed —
`gh api advisories -f ecosystem=pip -f affects=GitPython -f per_page=100 --paginate` returns **47**
(the same command without `per_page` returns only the first page of 30). `Head.checkout` appears in
two rows, one of which (`GHSA-w672-…`) is a withdrawn duplicate, leaving one substantive advisory:

- **`GHSA-hh9p-6wh2-4mfc` / CVE-2026-76217** — same method, but the **kwargs** path
  (`pathspec_from_file=…, pathspec_file_nul=True`), fixed in 3.1.58. That path is closed today; it is
  the positive control in every batch of this report. The **positional** path is not covered by it.

Neighbours, none overlapping:

- **`GHSA-3wxw-xv34-2frg` / CVE-2026-78679** — the same **class** (positional bypasses a kwargs-only
  guard) in a different method, `TagReference.create`, fixed in 3.1.59 by `1b0d2d9b`. That is the
  patch that did not come back to `head.py:286`.
- **`GHSA-956x-8gvw-wg5v` / CVE-2026-67323** — precedent for "a value placed before the `--` with no
  leading-dash check", in `Repo.iter_commits` / `Repo.blame`. Those sites now pass their positional
  to the guard; this one does not.
- **`GHSA-7545-fcxq-7j24` / CVE-2026-44243** — path traversal via ref names in the reference APIs.
  Different sink (filesystem path construction) and different impact (write and delete), but it
  establishes that attacker-influenced ref names is a premise this project has already accepted.

### No open fix proposal

Searched across three surfaces, because `gh search issues` excludes pull requests: `gh search prs`,
`gh search issues` and the raw `search/issues` API. **No open or closed issue or pull request
proposes passing the positional to the guard in `Head.checkout`.** The three PRs that touch this
guard (#2204, #2180, #2163) are all merged and none of them does it — #2204 is the PR that
introduced *both* call sites in this file, one checking its positional and one not. Full matrix in
`dup-check.md`.

### The project's own tests carry the same asymmetry

`test/test_refs.py` exercises the guard for both methods, and covers exactly the difference this
report is about:

- `HEAD.reset` — the **positional** is tested (lines 304-308).
- `Head.checkout` — only the **kwargs** path is tested (lines 282-291).

So the positional variant is a case the suite already knows how to write; it just was not written
for `checkout`. The docstring added by #2204 to `Head.checkout` states that `--pathspec-from-file`
requires opt-in via `allow_unsafe_options` — which is precisely the guarantee the positional path
does not deliver. Nothing in the project declares the positional acceptable here.

### Why the one-line fix works, which is not obvious

`Reference.__str__` returns `self.name`, not `self.path`. `Reference.name` strips the first two
path components (`reference.py:122-132`), so a `Head` constructed on
`refs/heads/--pathspec-from-file=/etc/passwd` passes `check_path` — the *path* does begin with
`refs/heads/` — while `str()` yields the bare option. Passing `[self]` to `_option_candidates` makes
the guard see that same serialised string, which is why the one-line change closes it.

## Evidence

| File | What it establishes |
|---|---|
| `poc.sh` | driver — runs all seven scenarios as one unit |
| `poc.log` | full transcript of the single reference run |
| `raw/00-versions-and-source.txt` | version under test is the published one; guard and sink present; `def checkout(` appears once, so the sink line is unambiguous |
| `raw/01-real-argv.txt` | real `git checkout` argv, captured by instrumenting `Git.execute` |
| `raw/02-refname-accepted-and-cloned.txt` | git accepts the refname; `Repo.clone_from` materialises it unasked |
| `raw/03-full-file-disclosure.txt` | 34 of 34 lines of `/etc/passwd` recovered |
| `raw/04-precision-control-reset-vs-checkout.txt` | `HEAD.reset` blocks what `Head.checkout` allows |
| `raw/05-six-line-consumer.txt` | six-line consumer, verbatim; leaks when the exception is logged and when it is uncaught |
| `raw/06-push-accepts-refname.txt` | a plain git server accepts the refname over `push` |
| `raw/07-blob-version-sweep.txt` | affected range by blob hash, tag by tag |
| `negative-controls.md` | what each control isolates and what would invalidate it |
| `evidence.sha256` | integrity of every raw file and script |

## Disclosure

Reported privately through GitHub private vulnerability reporting. No third-party systems were
touched: every repository in this report is a temporary local one, and all transport is `file://`.

## Summary

A project member with Write permission can delete an admin-tier link share on that project. The deletion authorization check reads the permission from an object populated only with URL IDs, rather than from the stored share. Its zero value is Read, so the check falls through to project Write permission instead of requiring Admin.

## Details

Affected endpoints:

- `DELETE /api/v1/projects/{project}/shares/{share}`
- `DELETE /api/v2/projects/{project}/shares/{share}`

Older v1 releases used `/lists/{list}/shares/{share}` before lists were renamed to projects.

In `pkg/routes/api/v2/link_sharing.go:156`, the delete handler passes `&models.LinkSharing{ID: in.ID, ProjectID: in.ProjectID}` to `handler.DoDelete`. The v1 generic handler likewise binds the URL IDs without loading the stored share.

`pkg/web/handler/core.go:185` calls `CanDelete` before `Delete`. `LinkSharing.CanDelete` delegates to `canDoLinkShare` in `pkg/models/link_sharing_permissions.go`. That helper loads the project but does not load the link share, then evaluates:

```go
if share.Permission == PermissionAdmin {
    return l.IsAdmin(s, a)
}
return l.CanWrite(s, a)
```

On deletion, `share.Permission` is its Go zero value, `PermissionRead` (0), even when the stored share grants `PermissionAdmin` (2). A Write member therefore passes authorization. `LinkSharing.Delete` subsequently deletes by share ID and project ID without checking the stored permission.

Create uses the requested permission and correctly rejects Write members creating admin shares. Share listing and by-ID reads are admin-gated in current main. There is no HTTP update route for link shares. Read-only members and link-share principals are rejected on deletion.

## Affected versions and verification

The admin-tier check was introduced in commit `56dbb564eae83f2453efd1049f55e9d099b5d346`, first included in v0.13, without loading the stored share on deletion. The affected range established by this review is `>= 0.13.0, <= 2.6.0`; versions before v0.13 have not been assessed here. The v2 route was added in `b10768506`, first included in v2.4.0.

The reporter states that both API versions were verified live against a local source build at `a881ac39eecd07575a5aede8e74727c28d5fd578` on September 7, 2026. Maintainer-side source review confirmed the mechanism in that commit, release v2.6.0, and upstream main at `a1a6ca48be142902f09fee62734310cb98a8c414`. The live proof of concept was not independently rerun during this triage. No patched version is available at draft creation.

## Impact

A Write collaborator can revoke an admin-tier access link on a project they can already write to. New consumers can no longer authenticate with that link. In versions with database-backed link-share JWT validation, deleting the share also immediately invalidates its existing sessions; the reporter observed HTTP 404 for a new hash exchange and HTTP 401 for an existing share token.

This is a bounded integrity and availability impact on external access to that project. It does not disclose data, grant Admin privileges, allow deletion of another project's shares, or permit the attacker to create a replacement admin share. The attacker must know or guess the numeric share ID; IDs are sequential.

Severity: Medium. CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization.

## Proof of concept

Use two regular accounts on an instance you control. Let `OWNER_TOKEN` and `WRITER_TOKEN` be their session tokens. Create a project as the owner, grant the second account Write permission (`permission: 1`), and create an admin-tier share as the owner (`permission: 2`). Let `PROJECT_ID` and `SHARE_ID` identify that project and share.

First, verify that the Write member cannot create an admin-tier share:

```sh
curl -i -X POST "$BASE/api/v2/projects/$PROJECT_ID/shares" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WRITER_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"permission":2}'
# Expected and reported: 403
```

Delete the owner's admin-tier share as the same Write member:

```sh
curl -i -X DELETE "$BASE/api/v2/projects/$PROJECT_ID/shares/$SHARE_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WRITER_TOKEN"
# Reported: 204; expected: 403 and the share remains intact
```

Recreate the admin-tier share as the owner and repeat with the v1 endpoint:

```sh
curl -i -X DELETE "$BASE/api/v1/projects/$PROJECT_ID/shares/$SHARE_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $WRITER_TOKEN"
# Reported: 200 with {"message":"Successfully deleted."}; expected: 403
```

With the collaborator downgraded to Read, deletion returns 403. These positive and negative controls were reported as verified live by the reporter.

## Recommended fix

For deletion, load the stored share scoped to both the requested share ID and project ID before authorizing. Require project Admin when the stored permission is Admin, and retain the intended Write rule for ordinary read/write shares. Preserve the existing cross-project constraint.

Keep creation authorization based on the requested tier. If update support is added, check both the stored tier and the requested new tier so neither demotion nor promotion can bypass the admin check.

Add regression coverage for a Write member being forbidden to delete an admin-tier share, an Admin being allowed, intended ordinary-share deletion, rejection of Read members and link-share principals, and mismatched project/share IDs. Cover both API versions.

## Related advisories

- [GHSA-f95f-77jx-fcjc / CVE-2026-33700](https://github.com/go-vikunja/vikunja/security/advisories/GHSA-f95f-77jx-fcjc) addressed cross-project deletion. Fix `654d2c704` constrained deletion by `project_id` but did not change the permission-tier check.
- [GHSA-qfwc-vx6f-3g6g](https://github.com/go-vikunja/vikunja/security/advisories/GHSA-qfwc-vx6f-3g6g) addressed share-hash disclosure through by-ID reads.
- [GHSA-8hp8-9fhr-pfm9](https://github.com/go-vikunja/vikunja/security/advisories/GHSA-8hp8-9fhr-pfm9) addressed share-hash disclosure through listing.
- [GHSA-96q5-xm3p-7m84 / CVE-2026-35594](https://github.com/go-vikunja/vikunja/security/advisories/GHSA-96q5-xm3p-7m84) addressed tokens remaining valid after deletion. That fix does not prevent unauthorized deletion.

## Credit

Reported via mail.

items.summary:
There is a local confidentiality issue in the default `FileSessionManager` storage behavior. By default it writes session data under `/tmp/strands/sessions` and relies on the process umask for directory and file permissions. On systems using the common `umask 022`, the session directories are `0755` and JSON files are `0644`, so other local users can read persisted agent session data.

This matters on shared developer machines, CI hosts, notebooks, jump boxes, and multi-user GPU servers. Session storage is intended to persist conversation/history/state, so it can contain prompts, model output, tool inputs/outputs, intermediate state, and secrets that pass through the agent.

Relevant code:
- `strands-py/src/strands/session/file_session_manager.py:58`: default storage path is `os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "strands/sessions")`.
- `strands-py/src/strands/session/file_session_manager.py:118`: creates parent directories without a private mode.
- `strands-py/src/strands/session/file_session_manager.py:121`: writes JSON files via normal `open(..., "w")`.
- `strands-py/src/strands/session/file_session_manager.py:131`: creates session directories without a private mode.

Local reproduction with `umask 022`:

```text
default_storage_dir= /tmp/strands/sessions
0o755 /tmp/strands/sessions
0o755 /tmp/strands/sessions/session_codex_perm_poc
0o644 /tmp/strands/sessions/session_codex_perm_poc/session.json
file_contains_secret= True
```

The fixture wrote a fake secret into the session dict to show that sensitive session fields are readable through the resulting file.

Suggested fixes:
- Use a private per-user data directory by default rather than `/tmp`, or create `/tmp/strands` and descendants with `0700`.
- Write session JSON atomically with `0600` permissions.
- Consider refusing to use an existing default storage directory if it is not owned by the current user or is group/world accessible.
- Document that callers should set `storage_dir` explicitly when they need shared storage.

This was reproduced on commit `dd7b41de38cb`.

items.summary:
### Summary

The built-in (but disabled by default) Brotli certificate decoder bounds the output buffer but accepts an input-selected history window. A header of five bytes can specify a 1 GiB window allocation. A peer can abort a process whose allocator cannot satisfy that request. A client must enable Brotli and connect to the peer; a server must enable Brotli and request a client certificate. Neither direction requires a trusted attacker certificate.

### Details

rustls calls `BrotliDecompress` which enables Brotli's large-window extension. rustls applies a limit to certificates, but this applies to the decompressed result, and not to any internal allocations the process requires.

### Impact

Client applications that enable the `brotli` feature will be vulnerable to malicious servers. Server applications that enable the `brotli` feature and enable client authentication will be vulnerable to malicious clients.

Potential for denial of service due to memory exhaustion from peers sending malicious Brotli-encoded certificates, for applications that enable Brotli decompression.

### Acknowledgement
Thanks to OpenAI [OutboundDisclosures@openai.com](mailto:OutboundDisclosures@openai.com) for the disclosure.

items.summary:
## Summary

The `FileSessionManager` defaults to storing session data in `/tmp/strands/sessions/` (a world-writable directory) using predictable file paths and a write pattern (`open(path + ".tmp", "w")` → `os.replace()`) that follows symbolic links. A local attacker can exploit this to overwrite arbitrary files or inject malicious session data for persistent prompt injection.

## Vulnerability Details

**Component:** `strands-py/src/strands/session/file_session_manager.py`

**Root Cause:**
1. Default storage directory is `tempfile.gettempdir() + "/strands/sessions/"` (line 58) — resolves to `/tmp/strands/sessions/` on Linux/macOS
2. The `_write_file()` method (lines 116-123) writes to a predictable `.tmp` path without symlink protection:
   ```python
   tmp = f"{path}.tmp"
   with open(tmp, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as f:
       json.dump(data, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
   os.replace(tmp, path)
   ```
3. `open()` follows symlinks — a pre-placed symlink at the `.tmp` path causes writes to an arbitrary target file
4. No integrity verification (HMAC/signature) on session files — tampered data is loaded as-is

## Attack Vectors

### 1. Arbitrary File Overwrite (Local Privilege Escalation)
1. Attacker pre-creates `/tmp/strands/sessions/session_<id>/` (or monitors for new directories via inotify)
2. Attacker creates a symlink: `session.json.tmp` → `/home/victim/.bashrc` (or any writable file)
3. Victim application writes session data → follows symlink → overwrites target file with JSON content
4. Attacker achieves code execution on next shell login (or targets `.ssh/authorized_keys`, cron files, etc.)

### 2. Persistent Prompt Injection via Session Tampering
1. Attacker writes crafted message files into the session directory
2. Victim application restores the session → loads attacker-controlled conversation history
3. Injected messages instruct the agent to execute attacker commands on every future interaction
4. No integrity check prevents this — the SDK trusts all session files at face value

## Impact

- **Arbitrary file overwrite** — local attacker can write attacker-controlled content to any file writable by the victim process
- **Local privilege escalation** — via overwriting shell configs, SSH keys, cron jobs, or systemd user services
- **Persistent agent compromise** — via session data injection, the agent follows attacker instructions indefinitely

## Reproduction

```python
import os, json, tempfile, shutil

# Setup: simulate the vulnerable write pattern
session_dir = "/tmp/strands/sessions/session_test/"
os.makedirs(session_dir, exist_ok=True)

# Attacker: create symlink at the .tmp write path
target_file = "/tmp/symlink_attack_proof.txt"
with open(target_file, "w") as f:
    f.write("ORIGINAL - should not be overwritten\n")

symlink_path = os.path.join(session_dir, "session.json.tmp")
if os.path.exists(symlink_path):
    os.unlink(symlink_path)
os.symlink(target_file, symlink_path)

# Victim: FileSessionManager._write_file() equivalent
with open(symlink_path, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="\n") as f:
    json.dump({"session_id": "test", "injected": True}, f, indent=2)

# Verify: target file overwritten
with open(target_file) as f:
    print(f"Target file content: {f.read()}")
    # Output: {"session_id": "test", "injected": true}

# Cleanup
os.unlink(symlink_path)
os.unlink(target_file)
shutil.rmtree(session_dir)
```

## Suggested Fix

1. **Use a user-private default directory** — `~/.strands/sessions/` or `$XDG_DATA_HOME/strands/sessions/` instead of `/tmp/`
2. **Use `os.open()` with `O_NOFOLLOW | O_CREAT | O_WRONLY`** — refuses to follow symlinks
3. **Use `tempfile.mkstemp()`** for atomic writes instead of predictable `.tmp` suffix
4. **Verify directory ownership** matches the current user before writing
5. **Add optional integrity verification** (HMAC) on session files to detect tampering
items.title: Strands Agents: Local Privilege Escalation via Symlink Attack in Default Session File Storage

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Drivers: hv: Don't reset VMBus connection state on error/exit paths

In two places, current code forces vmbus_connection.conn_state to
DISCONNECTED prior to calling vmbus_disconnect(). But vmbus_disconnect()
calls vmbus_initiate_unload(), which unloads the VMBus connection
only if the conn_state is CONNECTED. Consequently, the connection
remains and the Hyper-V host might continue to send messages or post
VMBus interrupts.

The problem was introduced in commit 74347a99e73ae ("x86/Hyper-V:
Unload vmbus channel in hv panic callback"), in that
vmbus_initiate_unload() started checking the current connection
state before doing the unload. This commit removed some occurrences
where conn_state was forced to DISCONNECTED, but these two remained,
apparently due to an oversight at the time.

Fix this by not forcing conn_state to DISCONNECTED during VMBus exit,
or if a failure occurs when establishing the connection in the first
place. Whatever value conn_state has at the time is then read by
vmbus_initiate_unload() to determine if there is a connection to
be unloaded.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

power: supply: core: prevent unregistering a power supply while a callback runs

Once a power supply is registered, its callbacks can immediately start
firing from other contexts, such as external_power_changed() triggered by
the TCPM stack. If a power supply is unregistered while the callback is
still running, the driver data can already be freed when the callback
tries to access it, leading to a use-after-free.

This happens e.g. when the hardware bus carrying the power supply device
malfunctions (e.g. I2C is hogged down by another malfunctioning device)
immediately after the power supply is registered, and thus the core is
still processing the callbacks which were queued up when the driver
starts the removal, leading in some cases to a kernel crash, e.g.:

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

vsock: treat TCP_CLOSING as once-established

Handle the TCP_ESTABLISHED -> TCP_CLOSING transition on OP_RST, which can
race with the connect loop. Immediately break and return 0 on
ESTABLISHED/CLOSING. The return value of connect() should reflect what
happened up to the point the connection was established or failed. Events
that occur afterwards must not affect it. E.g. even if OP_RW has already
set sk_err, connect() should still return 0, not ENOBUFS because of it.
Adapt the inaccurate comment above signal_pending().

Resetting a socket that is still present in connected_table can lead to
memory corruption. The reporter noted lost transports for in-flight skbs,
and I have reproduced crashes caused by re-insertion into connected_table.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/rds: don't let the rdma_cm destroy an id RDS still owns on route failure

rds_rdma_cm_event_handler_cmn() hands the return value of
rdma_resolve_route() straight back to the rdma_cm on
RDMA_CM_EVENT_ADDR_RESOLVED.  A synchronous failure there - -ENOMEM
from the route work allocation, an SA query that cannot be set up, a
RoCE route with no usable device - makes addr_handler() destroy the
id the event was delivered on.  That id is ic->i_cm_id, and nothing
clears the pointer: the connection sits in RDS_CONN_CONNECTING with a
freed id until its shutdown calls rdma_disconnect() and
rdma_destroy_id() on it.

The ROUTE_RESOLVED case already avoids this: rds_ib_cm_initiate_connect()
forces a zero return while ic->i_cm_id == cm_id, as the comment there
explains.  Do the same here - drop the connection and return 0 - so
the id stays RDS's to destroy from the shutdown, and the reconnect
gets a fresh one.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netlink: reset skb headers before unicast and multicast filtering

Socket filters can use SKF_NET_OFF and SKF_LL_OFF to read relative to
an skb's network and MAC headers. Netlink producers may reserve
headroom without resetting those headers, allowing a receiving socket's
filter to read data before the initialized message.

For example, IWPM HELLO replies are allocated with dev_alloc_skb(),
which reserves NET_SKB_PAD bytes. An unprivileged NETLINK_RDMA user can
attach a classic socket filter and disclose this headroom through the
length of the delivered reply. The resets in netlink_dump() do not help
because IWPM sends a separately allocated skb through netlink_unicast().

Reset both headers before running the receiver's filter in unicast and
broadcast delivery, as is already done for dump skbs. This also covers
other netlink producers that reserve headroom without changing their
allocation or message-building code.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

accel/rocket: clear rdev on device init failure

rocket_probe() stores the return value from rocket_device_init() in the
file-scoped rdev pointer before checking whether it is an error pointer.
If rocket_device_init() fails, rdev is left as an ERR_PTR.

The rdev pointer is also used as the marker for whether the shared rocket
device has already been initialized. A later core probe can therefore see
a non-NULL rdev, skip rocket_device_init(), and dereference the error
pointer when reading rdev->num_cores.

Save the error code and clear rdev before returning from the
rocket_device_init() failure path.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/xe: skip eviction of a BO with no resource

xe_evict_flags() switches on tbo->resource->mem_type to choose an
eviction placement. An xe BO can reach eviction with no ttm.resource,
e.g. an imported dma-buf BO whose resource was freed during teardown
while its attachment is still live: the exporter then invalidates it via
xe_dma_buf_move_notify() -> xe_bo_evict(), and the switch dereferences a
NULL resource and faults.

A BO with no resource has nothing placed or mapped, so there is nothing
to evict. Return an empty placement (num_placement = 0), mirroring the
handling already used for non-xe scatter-gather BOs just above;
ttm_bo_validate() then takes the pipeline-gutting path and returns 0.

Without the fix the xe_dma_buf@xe_test_dmabuf_move_notify_no_resource

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/xe/oa: Zero OA buffer at allocation

ttm_bo_type_kernel BOs are not guaranteed to be zeroed on allocation and
may contain data from previously freed pages. Since the OA buffer is
mmap'able by userspace, this can expose stale kernel memory contents.

Streams opened with DRM_XE_OA_PROPERTY_OA_DISABLED allocate the OA
buffer without calling xe_oa_init_oa_buffer(). Zero the buffer at
allocation to prevent information disclosure through mmap.

The existing zeroing in xe_oa_init_oa_buffer() remains necessary for
zero report-id/timestamp detection on enable/re-enable.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

scsi: target: Disable interrupts while holding delayed_cmd_lock

target_do_delayed_work() takes dev->delayed_cmd_lock with a plain
spin_lock(). It runs from system_percpu_wq, so interrupts stay enabled
while the lock is held. Every other acquisition of that lock uses
spin_lock_irqsave(): target_handle_task_attr() and
transport_complete_ordered_sync() in target_core_transport.c, and
target_non_ordered_release() in target_core_device.c.

That was safe while every caller of transport_complete_task_attr() ran
in process context: target_complete_ok_work() from target_completion_wq,
transport_complete_qf() from dev->qf_work_queue, and
transport_generic_request_failure() from the submit and execute paths.

Since commit 06933066d88a ("scsi: target: Add support for completing
commands from backend context") that is no longer true. With
complete_type=1 on a fabric that sets direct_compl_supp,
target_complete() runs target_complete_ok_work() inline in the backend's
completion context, which target_complete_cmd_with_sense() documents as
"May be called from interrupt context". For iblock that is the bio
end_io.

target_complete_ok_work() starts with transport_complete_task_attr(),
which takes delayed_cmd_lock in two ways:

 - Every ORDERED command is put on dev->delayed_cmd_list by
   target_handle_task_attr() and dispatched from there by
   target_do_delayed_work(), which marks it SCF_TASK_ORDERED_SYNC.  Its
   completion therefore goes through transport_complete_ordered_sync().

 - A SIMPLE command that completes while an ORDERED command is pending
   drops the last reference to the killed dev->non_ordered, and
   percpu_ref_put() then runs target_non_ordered_release() in the
   completing context.

Both take the lock and, if commands are waiting, call
schedule_work(&dev->delayed_cmd_work), which queues on system_percpu_wq,
i.e. on the CPU that took the completion. Further completions for the
same queue are typically delivered there too, so one arriving while the
work holds the lock spins on it forever.

Reaching this needs complete_type=1, which is not the default
(vhost-scsi, the only fabric with direct_compl_supp, defaults to
TARGET_QUEUE_COMPL), a backend whose I/O completes from interrupt
context, and ORDERED commands from the initiator. Linux virtio_scsi
guests send only VIRTIO_SCSI_S_SIMPLE and never take the ordered path;
any guest that uses the ORDERED task attribute, which vhost-scsi
accepts, does.

target_do_delayed_work() is a work item and always runs in process
context, so spin_lock_irq() is sufficient.

Found by inspection; no runtime report. A single ORDERED command goes
through both acquisitions, so with CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING the first one
completed through direct completion should produce an inconsistent lock
state report on delayed_cmd_lock (hardirq or softirq, depending on where
the backend completes).

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sched/core: Call wakeup_preempt() for queued tasks during class change

Paul reported recent RCU changes exposed a lost resched where CPU idles
with a rcutorture thread waiting while being completely runnable.

Dumping the rq state at the time of idling with runnable tasks showed
the following:

  rq->next_class = &fair_sched_class
  rq->nr_running = 1
  rq->cfs.h_nr_queued = 0
  rq->rt.rt_nr_running = 1

Although the waiting task was an RT task, "rq->next_class" did not point
to rt_sched_class and was stuck at the lower priority fair_sched_class.

Inspecting sched_change_end() revealed the following race with
__sched_setscheduler() for queued, but non-running tasks:

    CPU0                                   CPU1
    ====                                   ====

  __schedule()

    /*
     * rq->donor is a fair task that blocks.
     * rq->next_class = &fair_sched_class
     */

    rq_lock(rq0)

    pick_next_task()
      /* nr_running = 0 */
      pick_task_fair()
        sched_balance_newidle()
          raw_spin_rq_unlock(rq0)
                                    rq_lock(rq0)

                                    activate_task(rq0, p)
                                      /* p is a fair task */
                                      rq0->nr_running++;
                                      rq0->cfs.h_nr_queued++;
                                      wakeup_preempt(rq, p)
                                        rq->next_class = &fair_sched_class
                                        resched_curr()

                                    rq_unlock(rq0)

                                    __sched_setscheduler(p)
                                      /* p is moved to SCHED_RR */
                                      task_rq_lock(p)
                                      sched_change_begin()

				      rq0->cfs.h_nr_queued--;
				      rq0->rt.rt_nr_running++;

                                      sched_change_end()
                                        /*
                                         * p->on_rq = 1 (ctx->queued)
                                         * but p is not rq->donor
                                         * (!ctx->running) hence
                                         * resched_curr() is and
                                         * rq->next_class upgrade is
                                         * skipped.
                                         */

                                       task_rq_unlock()

          raw_spin_rq_lock(rq0)

          /*
           * rq->nr_running = 1
           * rq->cfs.h_nr_queued = 0
           * rq->rt.rt_nr_running = 1
           * rq->next_class = &fair_sched_class
           */

           if (rq->cfs.h_nr_queued && ...)
             /* Above is false */

           if (rq_modified_above(this_rq, &fair_sched_class))
             /* Also false since rq->next_class is still fair */

      /*
       * sched_balance_newidle() is considered to
       * have failed to pull any fair tasks and no
       * other wakeups were detected.
       */
       return NULL; /* pick_task_fair() */

    pick_task_idle()
      return rq->idle;

    next = rq->idle;

    /* Preemption indicators are lost */
    clear_tsk_need_resched(prev);
    clear_preempt_need_resched();

    rq->curr = rq->idle;

  !!! rq->idle switches in with rq->running == 1 but !need_resched() !!!

In simple words, enqueue, followed by a class change of the newly queued
task goes unnoticed in rq->next_class indicator and
sched_balance_newidle() sees no fair task, nor any higher priority task
enqueued.

The above sequence will lead to CPU idling with a runnable task on the
CPU.

Call wakeup_preempt() for ctx->queued cases in sched_change_end() to
re-evaluate rq->next_class after class change (ENQUEUE_CLASS) and set
the NEED_RESCHED indicator accordingly.

Newidle balance will correctly see an enqueue of a higher priority
t

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ocfs2/dlm: Protect the recovery list during debugfs reads

Recovery participant records must remain alive while debug_state_print()
walks reco.node_data and formats their fields. The formatter holds
dlm->spinlock, but the recovery participant list is protected by
dlm_reco_state_lock. In particular, dlm_destroy_recovery_area() detaches
the list under dlm_reco_state_lock and frees the detached records after
releasing it. A concurrent debugfs open can therefore read freed memory.

Protect the participant traversal and field reads in debug_state_print()
with dlm_reco_state_lock, matching the existing list writers. This also
serializes the traversal against list_add_tail() during recovery-area
initialization. Make the existing lock available to the debug code
through dlmcommon.h; the lock remains internal to the OCFS2 DLM module.

Release dlm->spinlock after formatting the other domain state and before
acquiring dlm_reco_state_lock, so the debug reader does not nest the two
locks. Leave recovery list insertion, detachment and freeing unchanged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

pipe: preserve existing fasync readers on writer setup failure

F_SETFL and FIOASYNC decide whether to invoke ->fasync() before
pipe_fasync() takes pipe->mutex. Two enables of one O_RDWR FIFO can
therefore both enter the callback.

fasync_helper() allocates before checking for an existing entry. If the
first enable installs both entries, a second enable can update the
reader entry and then fail the allocation for the writer entry. The
error path removes the pre-existing reader entry, clearing FASYNC while
the writer entry remains registered. __fput() then skips ->fasync(), so a
later pipe notification can dereference the freed file or its f_owner.
An unprivileged memory-pressure reproducer triggers a KASAN
slab-use-after-free in send_sigio() through this path.

Keep the reader helper's result and undo the registration only if this
call added it. The pipe mutex serializes changes to both lists, so a
failed new registration still removes its reader, while a failed
duplicate preserves the existing registrations and FASYNC. Successful
duplicate enables continue to update fa_fd as before.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

scsi: libsas: Fix SMP IO deadlock during HA resume

smp_execute_task_sg() calls pm_runtime_get_sync() on the host before
issuing an SMP command. When that command is itself issued from the HA
resume path, the get_sync() deadlocks: it waits for the ongoing resume
(the device is RPM_RESUMING), while the resume is blocked in
sas_drain_work() waiting for that same SMP IO to complete.

The deadlock needs an expander-attached SATA disk. During
sas_resume_ha() -> sas_drain_work(), DISCE_RESUME -> sas_resume_sata()
-> ata_sas_port_resume() requests ATA_EH_RESET, and the hard reset for
such a disk is done via SMP PHY CONTROL (sas_ata_hard_reset() ->
sas_phy_reset() -> sas_smp_phy_control() ->
smp_execute_task_sg()). Direct-attached SATA resets through
lldd_control_phy() and SSP devices use TMFs, so neither hits this.

Replace the get_sync()/put_sync() pair with
pm_runtime_get_noresume()/pm_runtime_put(). smp_execute_task_sg() only
needs to hold off autosuspend while the SMP is in flight, and it must
not try to resume the host: a sync resume issued from the HA resume path
itself is what deadlocks, and by the time sas_resume_ha() runs, hw_init
has already reinitialized the hardware, so the device is accessible
without one.

The usage reference is still required. Discovery work normally runs
inside an event worker's PM reference, taken at sas_notify_port_event()
notify time and held until the handler has flushed the disco
queue. sas_rediscover_ex_phy() however requeues DISCE_REVALIDATE_DOMAIN
from within the revalidation worker itself, and flush_workqueue() does
not wait for work items queued during execution, so that chained
revalidation runs with no outer PM reference - without the
get_noresume(), its SMP could race autosuspend.

For the BSG path, sas_smp_handler() is the only caller which may find
the host autosuspended: expander SMP requests do not go through any SCSI
device request queue, so nothing else in that path holds the host
awake. Resume it there with pm_runtime_resume_and_get() and check the
result.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

netlink: avoid hashing the network namespace pointer

The netlink rhashtable key includes a raw struct net pointer and a
user-controlled port ID. Both /proc/net/netlink and socket diagnostics
expose the table's bucket order. By binding and rebinding chosen
NETLINK_USERSOCK port IDs, an unprivileged reader can distinguish equal
buckets and recover the low bits of the Jenkins hash. Its 32-bit seed
and the limited set of kernel-image slides can then be searched offline
to recover the address of init_net.

Use the namespace's unique, non-address net_cookie in the comparison
key instead. It is assigned before the per-net initializers run and
remains unchanged for the namespace's lifetime. The lookup key and
object hash are still built by netlink_compare_arg_init(), keeping
lookup, insertion, removal and rehashing consistent while preserving
namespace separation. Neither public table walker needs to change.

Reading the socket's namespace cookie in netlink_compare() is safe
under RCU, including during namespace teardown. netlink_release()
removes the socket from the hash table and defers its final put with
call_rcu(). cleanup_net() runs the per-net exit methods and waits for
outstanding RCU callbacks with rcu_barrier() before freeing namespace
storage.

Unlike ns.ns_id, net_cookie is also available and initialized during
setup_net() in older stable kernels, making the change straightforward
to backport to v5.15 and later.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: bcmgenet: unshare the skb before writing the control block

bcmgenet stores first_cb, last_cb and bytes_sent in the skb control
block and reads them back on completion to free the skb and credit BQL.
ether_setup() leaves IFF_TX_SKB_SHARING set, so the stack can resubmit
a shared skb that is still in the ring. The next transmit overwrites
last_cb, so the earlier slots complete without crediting their bytes
and BQL stalls the queue until the watchdog resets it.

Unshare the skb before writing the control block.

Reproduce with pktgen in clone_skb mode, which hands the driver the same
skb while earlier copies are still in the ring:

  modprobe pktgen
  pg=/proc/net/pktgen
  echo "add_device eth0" > $pg/kpktgend_0
  echo "dst_mac AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF" > $pg/eth0
  echo "dst 192.0.2.1" > $pg/eth0
  echo "clone_skb 8" > $pg/eth0
  echo "count 0" > $pg/eth0
  echo start > $pg/pgctrl &
  sleep 5
  echo stop > $pg/pgctrl
  wait
  cat /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/tx-0/byte_queue_limits/inflight

inflight stays nonzero on the now idle queue. clone_skb 0 leaves it at
zero.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

calipso: keep BIG TCP payload_len in calipso_skbuff_setattr()

calipso_skbuff_setattr() adjusts payload_len by the length of the
option it inserts or resizes:

	payload = ntohs(ip6_hdr->payload_len);
	ip6_hdr->payload_len = htons(payload + len_delta);

GRO can build BIG TCP packets larger than IPV6_MAXPLEN, and stores
payload_len == 0 for them; ipv6_payload_len() then falls back to
skb->len.  For such a packet forwarded to a destination mapped to
CALIPSO, the code above writes len_delta (or 65536 + len_delta when
shrinking) into payload_len, and ipv6_payload_len() no longer falls
back to skb->len.  nf_tables, conntrack and sch_cake rely on it.

The same arithmetic also wraps when a packet grows past IPV6_MAXPLEN,
and a BIG TCP packet that shrinks below IPV6_MAXPLEN should get its
real length back.

Set payload_len from the skb length with ipv6_set_payload_len(), which
stores 0 above IPV6_MAXPLEN and the real length otherwise, as
ipv6_gro_complete() does.  The network header was just reset to
skb->data, so skb->len - sizeof(*ip6_hdr) is the payload length.

Tested on one kernel (arm64, QEMU) with SELinux permissive, a minimal
mdp-generated policy (network_peer_controls=1), "netlabelctl calipso
add pass doi:16" and a NetLabel mapping of fd00:2::/64 to CALIPSO
DOI 16.  calipso_skbuff_setattr() was called through
netlbl_skbuff_setattr() from a test-only debugfs hook (not part of
this patch) adding a level-only label; payload_len after the call:

  case                         before fix   after fix   real length
  1000, unlabeled                    1016        1016          1016
  70000 GSO, payload_len 0             16           0         70016
  65530 GSO, grows past MAXPLEN        10           0         65546
  65540 GSO with a 24 byte hop
  header, shrinks below MAXPLEN     65528       65532         65532
  1000 with a 24 byte hop header      992         992           992

(0 means ipv6_payload_len() returns the real length.)  On the forward
path, with a client injecting unlabeled UDP through a router to a
server, the router adds the CALIPSO option and the server delivers all
datagrams (Udp6InDatagrams 5, Ip6InTruncatedPkts 0) with this patch.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

gpio: mxc: fix race between chained IRQ handler install and probe completion

mxc_update_irq_chained_handler() is called before the IRQ domain, the
generic IRQ chip, and the port list entry are set up. If an interrupt
arrives in that window:

 - mx3_gpio_irq_handler() calls generic_handle_domain_irq() with
   port->domain still NULL.
 - mx2_gpio_irq_handler() walks mxc_gpio_ports, but the port has not
   been added to the list yet.

(gpio_generic_chip_init(), devm_gpiochip_add_data(),
irq_domain_create_legacy(), or mxc_gpio_init_gc()) fail, the error

that points at freed memory.

after list_add_tail(), so the handler is never live while the data
structures it touches are incomplete, and is never installed if probe
fails.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: stmmac: dwmac1000: clear the RGMII status interrupt

Since commit 2e2c878a3141 ("net: stmmac: remove SGMII/RGMII/SMII
interrupt handling") nothing on the RGMII path reads GMAC_RGSMIIIS, so
RGSMIIIS stays pending behind GMAC_INT_MASK from the first link change
on. stmmac_resume() resets the MAC in stmmac_hw_setup(); the reset sets
GMAC_INT_MASK to 0 until dwmac1000_core_init() writes the mask again,
and the pending status storms the line:

  dwmac_dma_interrupt: unexpected status 04000000

A register dump at the first message on ODROID-HC4 showed it:

  core int_status 00000001 int_mask 00000000 pmt 00000000 rgsmiiis 0000000d

When the resume thread runs on the CPU that takes the MAC interrupt,
the storm starves it: a soft lockup, then a watchdog reset or a hang.

masked, as the driver did before 2e2c878a3141; the read clears it.

Wake-on-LAN resume from s2idle with the resume thread and the MAC
interrupt on one CPU: Helios64 (dwmac-rk), 7.3-rc6, soft-locked in 3 of
3 resumes without a fix and in 0 of 10 with this patch; it ran with an
out-of-tree dwmac-rk change that keeps the GMAC powered across suspend.

fix on a 7.3-rc5 build. irq_rgmii_n went up by one per resume.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

perf: Fix perf_pmu_migrate_context() leaving events behind

__perf_pmu_remove() walks the group leaders of a CPU and PMU with
perf_event_groups_for_cpu_pmu(), removing each one as it goes.
perf_remove_from_context() takes the leader out of the groups rbtree,
after which rb_next() on that node returns NULL, prematurely ending the
walk. Other groups stay behind in the source context.

On CPU hotplug, they are then torn down with the dying CPU. They keep
running until teardown, while the PMU's interrupt and migrated events
are on a new CPU, which drivers rely on never happening.

pmu_ctx.

x86/insn-eval: Fix shadowed segment index in get_seg_reg_override_idx()

Commit 45e1dccc0653 ("x86/insn: Simplify for_each_insn_prefix()") made
for_each_insn_prefix() declare its own loop counter named idx.
get_seg_reg_override_idx() keeps its result in a local of the same name,
so the assignments in the loop body now write the loop counter:

 - the function always returns INAT_SEG_REG_DEFAULT, so FS and GS
   overrides are ignored;

 - a CS override sets the counter to INAT_SEG_REG_CS (2), the increment
   makes it 3, and prefixes.bytes[3] holds the last prefix, 0x2e again,
   so the loop never terminates.

SGDT, SIDT or SMSW with a memory operand and a CS prefix leaves the task
spinning in the kernel, never returning to user space, with a SIGKILL
that is never delivered.  Any user can thus tie up CPUs until reboot.
With an FS or GS prefix, the emulated result is written to the wrong
address.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

firewire: core: fix race condition in split transaction handling

For a split transaction, either fw_core_handle_response() or
split_transaction_timeout_callback() may manipulate the same transaction
entry in the pending transaction list. The return value of timer_delete()
is used to determine which function handles the entry. If the transaction
is a split transaction and timer_delete() returns zero, the timeout
callback may already be running. In this case, the response handler must
leave the entry in the list for the timeout callback to remove.

A previous code refactoring broke this behavior, introducing a race
condition in which both functions could process the same transaction.
This could lead to a use-after-free on the transaction initiator side.

Fix the regression by ensuring that the response handler does not process
the transaction when timer_delete() returns zero. The timeout callback is
responsible for removing the entry from the pending transaction list.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

accel/rocket: search every core slot when a core is removed

rocket_remove() decrements rdev->num_cores for each core it removes,
while find_core_for_dev() searches slots 0 to num_cores - 1. Unbinding
the cores in the order they were bound therefore loses the last one: by
the time it is removed the search range has already shrunk past its
slot, so find_core_for_dev() returns -1 and rocket_remove() gives up
without doing anything.

num_cores never reaches zero, rocket_device_fini() never runs, and the
file-scoped rdev keeps pointing at a device that is going away. Binding
the cores again starts from that stale count, because rocket_probe()
takes rdev->num_cores as the slot to fill. On an RK3588, which describes
three cores, the second round lands on slots 1, 2 and 3 while rdev->cores
was allocated with room for three:

  rocket fdab0000.npu: Rockchip NPU core 1 version: 1179210309
  rocket fdac0000.npu: Rockchip NPU core 2 version: 1179210309
  rocket fdad0000.npu: Rockchip NPU core 3 version: 1179210309

The write to rdev->cores[3] is past the end of the array.

Nothing in tree reads the core array often enough to notice, so the
overrun is silent today. It turned up while testing a devfreq series on
top of this, where a worker walks every core a few times a second, and
UBSAN caught the first bool it read out of the overrun entry:

  UBSAN: invalid-load in drivers/accel/rocket/rocket_devfreq.c:47:10
  load of value 5 is not a valid value for type '_Bool'
  Workqueue: devfreq_wq devfreq_monitor

Record how many slots were allocated and search all of them. Every core
is then found on removal, num_cores reaches zero, the device is torn down
and a later bind starts from a clean rdev.

This does not make unbinding a single core out of several work. probe
still takes num_cores as the slot to fill, so rebinding one core while
its siblings stay bound would write over a slot that is already in use,
and rocket_open() still reaches for cores[0] whether or not anything is
there. Both of those want more thought than a fix should carry.

Found by unbinding and rebinding all three cores on an Orange Pi 5 Plus.
With this applied, 25 unbind/rebind rounds and 5 module unload/reload
rounds run clean there: the cores land in slots 0, 1 and 2 every time,
whichever order they are bound in, and the shared supply goes back to a
single user after each round.

rocket_remove() decrements num_cores for every core it removes. Unbind a
core that is not the last one and the cores behind it fall outside the
search, so sched_to_core() returns NULL for a core that is still bound and
still running jobs. Neither caller checks the result:

  rocket_job_run():      rocket_fence_create(core), core->dev
  rocket_job_timedout(): dev_err(core->dev, "NPU job timed out")

Unbinding the middle core of the three on an RK3588 while three clients are
submitting to all of them faults twice, once from the surviving core's
job queue and once from its reset work:

  KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000220-0x0000000000000227]
  Workqueue: fdad0000.npu drm_sched_run_job_work [gpu_sched]
  pc : rocket_job_run+0x234/0x838 [rocket]
  Call trace:
   rocket_job_run+0x234/0x838 [rocket]
   drm_sched_run_job_work+0x2cc/0xad8 [gpu_sched]
   process_one_work+0x640/0x14f0

  KASAN: null-ptr-deref in range [0x0000000000000000-0x0000000000000007]
  Workqueue: rocket-reset-2 drm_sched_job_timedout [gpu_sched]
  pc : rocket_job_timedout+0xf0/0x1e0 [rocket]
  Call trace:
   rocket_job_timedout+0xf0/0x1e0 [rocket]
   drm_sched_job_timedout+0x188/0x6a0 [gpu_sched]

Both are the third core: the workqueue names are its device and its
core->index, and it was left at slot 2 while num_cores had dropped to 2.

Search all the slots that were allocated, the way find_core_for_dev() now
does. A core that is still bound is then found, and the two callers get
the pointer they already assume they have.

This does not make unbinding one core out of several safe. An open client
keeps an entity pointing at the scheduler of the core that went away:
drm_sched reports it as not ready for every job that lands on it, and the
client waits in dma_fence_default_wait for a fence that will never signal.
Stopping the NULL dereference is what belongs in a fix; the rest wants
more thought.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ASoC: SOF: ipc4-topology: Fix shift-out-of-bounds for aggregated ALH capture

When ch_count is smaller than blob->alh_cfg.device_count (e.g. a mono
capture stream, such as a SmartMic, aggregated across multiple SDW
links), step = ch_count / blob->alh_cfg.device_count truncates to 0.
The subsequent GENMASK(step - 1, 0) then underflows step - 1 (u32) to
UINT_MAX, causing GENMASK()'s internal shift to use an out-of-bounds
exponent:

  UBSAN: shift-out-of-bounds in sound/soc/sof/ipc4-topology.c:2363:13
  shift exponent 18446744069414584384 is too large for 64-bit type 'long unsigned int'

Treat ch_count < device_count the same way as the existing "channels
equal to output reference channels" case: apply the same ch_mask to
every aggregated device instead of trying to split channels that
can't be evenly divided.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

autofs: ignore notification errors from a replaced pipe

autofs_notify_daemon() takes a reference to the current notification
pipe under wq_mutex, then drops the mutex before writing the request. The
write can block while the daemon enters catatonic mode and installs a
replacement pipe.

If the old pipe's reader is then closed, the delayed write returns -EPIPE
and the generic error path enters catatonic mode again. That transition
acts on the current superblock state, closes the replacement pipe, and
releases the new daemon generation's wait queues.

Only enter catatonic mode when the pipe which failed is still the current
pipe. Factor the already-locked transition so the identity check and state
change are atomic with respect to another replacement.

This was reproduced on v7.3-rc5-337-gff47652a4b66c in a local QEMU guest.
An unprivileged UID 65534 lookup filled the old packet pipe before a
normal CATATONIC/SETPIPEFD restart. On the unmodified kernel, the new pipe
received HUP and both a pending victim lookup and a later lookup failed
with ENOENT in two out of two fresh-mount runs.

With this change, the new pipe remained active, received an intact
304-byte request, and both victim lookups completed in two out of two
runs. Normal lookup and restart-without-a-blocked-writer controls passed.
No KASAN, oops, refcount, or lock diagnostic was observed. A source
reproducer and complete local logs are available privately on request.

The demonstrated impact is limited to denial of a shared autofs service
during a legitimate daemon restart. No memory corruption, information leak,
privilege escalation, or code execution primitive was observed.
